summary: Reports the work of a committee that cleaned up problems in the original Host-Host Protocol, the rules the first ARPANET computers used to set up connections and control data flow. It lists agreed changes to the protocol and discusses at length what a byte means for a connection. It replaced the committee's earlier report in RFC 102.

plainLanguage.summary: RFC 107 records the fixes a committee agreed on for the first ARPANET Host-Host Protocol, the rules the earliest network computers used to open connections and control data flow. It changes connections from bit streams to byte streams, rewrites the message format, and adds reset and flow-control rules. It replaced the committee's earlier report in RFC 102.

subtitle: A 1971 committee's fixes to the first ARPANET Host-Host Protocol, from byte streams to new flow control.

tldr.problem: The original Host-Host Protocol treated a connection as a bare bit stream, which forced expensive shifting on both sides, and it had flow control and control-message quirks.
tldr.mechanism: The committee turned connections into byte streams with a size S, changed the message format, added reset commands RST and RRP, replaced the Cease mechanism with separate message and bit allocations, and moved control traffic to link 0.
tldr.outcome: This RFC entirely supersedes RFC 102 and officially modifies Document #1; it was later updated by RFC 111, RFC 124, RFC 132, RFC 154 and RFC 179.

today: RFC 107 has an unknown status. It supersedes RFC 102 and was later updated by RFC 111, RFC 124, RFC 132, RFC 154 and RFC 179.

sections.title: The Glitch Cleaning Committee
sections.content:
The Host-Host Protocol Glitch Cleaning Committee met for the second time at UCLA on 8 and 9 March 1971, after canvassing the network community. The first meeting, which spent most of its time on the interrupt mechanism, is documented in RFC 102. This RFC entirely supersedes RFC 102 and is an official modification of Document #1, the original Host-Host Protocol specification; a revision of Document #1 was to follow.

NCP implementers were told to incorporate the changes as soon as possible and to report an estimated ready date to Steve Crocker or his secretary. The second meeting spent almost all of its time on the notion of bytes, which is discussed after the list of modifications.
sections.plainLanguage: A committee of network engineers met twice to fix unclear parts of the first rules for connections between ARPANET computers. This RFC lists the fixes they agreed on and replaces their earlier report.

sections.title: Byte Streams and Message Format
sections.content:
A connection has been a bit stream; henceforth it is a byte stream, with the byte size S named in the STR command and in each message. The size must satisfy 1 <= S <= 255, is chosen by third-level protocol, stays constant for the life of the connection, and each message must contain a whole number of text bytes.

The new message format carries fields S (8 bits, the byte size, which must match the size in the STR that created the connection) and C (16 bits, the number of bytes in the text). A zero C has no meaning but is legal. Fields M1 and M2 are 8 bits each and must be zero, and M3, zero or more bits, must be all zero and may pad the message out to a word boundary, followed by padding. The text field starts 72 bits after the start of the message and consists of C bytes of S bits each.

The partition of the byte stream into messages is an artifact of the subnet, and no semantic content attaches to message boundaries. A message with a zero byte count is legal but uses up resource allocation. A receiver may not expect third-level control information to line up with message boundaries, and no data type is defined in the second-level protocol.
sections.plainLanguage: Data now moves in agreed-size bytes instead of single bits. Every message states the byte size and how many bytes it carries. Where one message ends carries no meaning for the program, so records and data types cannot depend on message boundaries.

sections.title: Reset, Flow Control and Control Links
sections.content:
Two new one-bit control commands were added: RST (reset) tells the receiving host to purge its NCP tables of all entries that arose from the host that sent the RST, and the host receiving it acknowledges with RRP (reset reply). The host that sent the RST may then request connections after receiving either an RST or an RRP in return.

Flow control changes in two ways. The Cease mechanism is discontinued, and the Imps stop recognizing and generating the 10HI, 11HI and 12HI messages. Allocation now deals with two quantities, messages and bits, allocated separately by the receiver. Each side keeps a 16-bit unsigned counter for messages and a 32-bit unsigned counter for bits. The sender may not send if either counter would go below zero, and the receiver may not raise the current message allocation above the maximum of the 16-bit counter or the current bit allocation above the maximum of the 32-bit counter. The text length of a message is S times C. The ALL, GVB and RET commands treat both quantities; the new GVB has four eight-bit fields, with fM and fB naming how much of the message and bit allocation to return, read as 128ths of the current allocation for values 0 to 128 and as all of it for 128 to 255.

The control link is changed to link 0, and link 1 is not to be used, so the old and new protocols can coexist. Control messages use the normal message format with byte size 8, may not carry more than 120 bytes of text, and must contain whole control commands. Links are assigned as follows: 0 is the control link, 1 is the old protocol's control link, to be phased out, 2 to 31 are for connections, 32 to 190 are reserved, 191 is only for measurement work under the network measurement center at UCLA, and 192 to 255 are available for private experimental use. The ECO and ERP commands become fixed at 16 bits, and ERR at 96 bits: 8 bits of op code, 8 bits of error code and 80 bits of text, enough for the longest non-ERR control command.
sections.plainLanguage: A reset command lets one computer tell another to forget everything it remembers about it. Flow control now counts messages and bits separately, and the sender may spend only what the receiver has granted. Dedicated control traffic moves to link 0.

sections.title: Why Bytes? The Committee's Discussion
sections.content:
Bit streams gave maximum generality and minimum efficiency. Receiving hosts had to do expensive shifting to concatenate the texts of successive messages, and sending hosts often had to shift text to align it on word boundaries. A sending NCP was also prohibited from holding any text if it could send even one bit, to prevent deadlock: two processes that each produce one bit of output per bit of input could stall each other if a waiting bit were delayed.

These considerations led to a transmission unit the NCPs would know about, which the committee concluded should be indivisible and fairly small; that notion turned out to be synonymous with the byte, so the term transmission unit was dropped. For character-oriented interaction an 8-bit unit seemed reasonable; for line-oriented interaction the line itself or a character; for file transfer a multiple of both machines' word lengths, though a too-large unit would leave a short final piece.

The discussion also noted two byte sizes may exist on one connection: size S from the sending process to the sending NCP, which the protocol carries, and a possibly different size R from the receiving NCP to the receiving process, which only decides how often the NCP wakes the user process; UCSB, storing binary files, might receive 32-bit increments while a host sends 36-bit bytes. A receiver may refuse a connection because of the proffered byte size. Conceptually NCPs handle all byte sizes, and the committee strongly suggests they do, though small hosts may restrict the variety based on what their third-level programs need.
sections.plainLanguage: The committee explains why sending single bits was slow and could stall both sides, and why they settled on small indivisible bytes. The sending side's byte size is a protocol matter; the receiving side may wake its program at a different, local rhythm.
